Immigrant Residential Segregation in Europe: A
Comparative Study of Spatial Segregation Patterns in Urban
Areas across 30 Countries
Tobias R ¨uttenauer1,2,†, Kasimir Dederichs2,†, David Kretschmer2,†
1Social Research Institute, University College London
2Nuffield College, University of Oxford
†All authors contributed equally
Abstract
Immigrant residential segregation can profoundly shape access to opportunities, immigrant
integration, and inter-group relations. Yet we lack systematic evidence on how segregation
varies across Europe, and what structural factors are associated with these patterns. This
study addresses the gap by focusing on two questions: (i) how does immigrant-native seg-
regation vary across urban areas in Europe, and (ii) which urban area- and country-level
characteristics are consistently linked to segregation?
Using harmonised 1×1 km grid-level data from the 2021/22 census, we calculate spatially
weighted Dissimilarity Indices for all 717 Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) across 30 European
countries. We combine these measures with rich data on demographics, the economy, housing,
immigrant populations, and policy. To identify robust correlates of segregation, we apply a
Specification Curve Analysis across 16,164 regression models.
Segregation is higher in Western and Northern Europe compared to most of Eastern and
Southern Europe. Moreover, we show that segregation is heavily driven by macro-spatial dy-
namics between diverse urban cores and relatively homogeneous suburban areas. At the urban
area level, segregation is systematically linked to the demographic composition and spatial dis-
tribution of the local population, economic conditions, housing market characteristics, as well
as the composition of the immigrant population. At the national level, established immigrant
destinations are more segregated, while migration and integration policies are not consistently
linked to segregation.
These findings offer the most comprehensive comparative assessment of immigrant segre-
gation across Europe to date, revealing how structural conditions relate to spatial integration.

1 Introduction and Background
Residential segregation has significant implications for the opportunities available to minority
groups and for broader social cohesion. For instance, segregation restricts contact opportunities
in neighbourhoods, limits the diversity of schools, community organizations, and public amenities
(Boterman and Musterd, 2016; Wiertz, 2016), and constrains access to resources and opportunities
(Chetty et al., 2016; Sharkey and Faber, 2014; Wodtke et al., 2023). A large body of research has
documented racial segregation in the United States (Elbers, 2024; Lee et al., 2008; Lichter et al.,
2015; Logan and Alba, 1993; Logan and Parman, 2025; Massey and Denton, 1988; Roberto and
Korver-Glenn, 2021) and immigrant segregation in European countries (Benassi et al., 2020; Cat-
ney et al., 2023; Lichter et al., 2019; Marci´ nczak et al., 2023; Musterd, 2005; R ¨uttenauer, 2022;
Sleutjes et al., 2018; Spierenburg et al., 2023; Teltemann et al., 2015).
Traditionally, research has focused on three key causes of segregation: (i) preferences for living
near in-group members (Bruch and Mare, 2006; Crowder and South, 2008; Krysan et al., 2009;
Liebe et al., 2023), (ii) socio-economic disparities that lead to unequal housing budgets and sorting
(Alba et al., 1999; Charles, 2003; Lersch, 2013), as well as (iii) discrimination in the housing
market (Auspurg et al., 2019; Desmond and Wilmers, 2019; Faber, 2020; Heath and Di Stasio,
2019; Quillian et al., 2020; Rosen et al., 2021). While each cause is important in its own, recent
work also highlights their interdependence and the role of structural barriers that simultaneously
shape preferences, economic inequalities, and discriminatory practices (Faber, 2020; Krysan and
Crowder, 2017; Lichter et al., 2024; Parisi et al., 2025). This underscores the key role that structural
urban characteristics may play in shaping segregation. Such urban area correlates of segregation
have been the focus of several studies (Benassi et al., 2020; Iceland and Scopilliti, 2008; Kye and
Halpern-Manners, 2023; Lichter et al., 2024; Marci´ nczak et al., 2023; Parisi et al., 2025). They
have investigated how urban demographics, spatial layouts, institutional arrangements, and other
characteristics are linked to segregation levels. In the US, studies document higher segregation
in metropolitan areas with larger populations, higher minority shares, newer housing stock, and
elevated poverty rates (Iceland and Scopilliti, 2008; Kye and Halpern-Manners, 2023; Lichter et al.,
2024, 2015; Parisi et al., 2025). Comparative studies also underscore the role of the urban–suburban
divide, with minorities often over-represented in urban cores (Elbers, 2024; Logan et al., 2023).
In Europe, comparative studies have similarly compared cities and explored structural correlates
of immigrant segregation (Andersson et al., 2018; Benassi et al., 2020, 2023; Johnston et al., 2007;
Koopmans, 2010; Lichter et al., 2019; Marci´ nczak et al., 2023; Musterd, 2005). These studies show,
for example, that British cities tend to be more segregated than those in continental Europe, and
that segregation is stronger among non-European vis-` a-vis European immigrants (Benassi et al.,
2020; Koopmans, 2010; Marci´ nczak et al., 2023; Musterd, 2005). Furthermore, findings suggest
that segregation is stronger in urban areas with larger populations and a higher proportion of
immigrants, and weaker in cities with wealthier and more educated populations (Benassi et al.,
2020; Marci´ nczak et al., 2023).
Although Europe offers a particularly compelling case for comparative research due to its
diverse urban landscapes and diverse policy contexts, previous comparative studies are based on
2

a set of only 5-8 European countries and data from 2011 or earlier. As a result, the majority
of European countries – particularly those in Eastern and Southern Europe – have not yet been
included in comparative studies, and recent immigration flows have not been taken into account.
Moreover, each of the prior studies has considered only a narrow set of macro-level segregation
correlates, preventing a comprehensive and up-to-date assessment of patterns and correlates of
segregation across Europe. These limitations largely stem from data constraints, such as (a)
inconsistent definitions of immigrant status across countries (e.g., citizenship vs. country of birth),
(b) differences in the size and resolution of administrative spatial units, and (c) limited availability
of harmonised country- and urban-level characteristics.
We address these limitations and provides a comprehensive analysis of immigrant residential
segregation across Europe. We ask: (i) how does the level of immigrant segregation vary across
European urban areas, and (ii) which characteristics of urban areas and national contexts are
associated with segregation levels? Our analysis covers all 717 Functional Urban Areas (FUAs)
across 30 European countries. FUAs are standardised spatial units that include city centres and
surrounding commuting zones, comparable to metropolitan areas in the US. Using 1×1 km grid
cell data from the 2021/22 European census, we provide segregation indices for each FUA. The
harmonised definition of spatial units and the harmonised measure of migration status ensure
comparability across different national contexts in Europe. Our assessment of all urban areas across
30 countries significantly expands the geographical scope of existing research, for the first time
mapping segregation patterns for most of the European continent. It also provides an important
update to research based on the 2011 census.
We link these segregation indices to a rich, original dataset with information on 40 FUA- and
country-level indicators drawn from Eurostat, the OECD, the UN, and other sources. This allows
us to analyse how segregation is linked to the local population and its demographics, economic
conditions, housing market characteristics, immigrant inflow and composition, and country-level
policies and migration histories.
Given the large number of covariates and plausible ways to specify models, we do not provide
estimates for associations from a single and necessarily debatable model specification. Instead, we
employ Specification Curve Analysis (SCA; Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson 2020) to estimate
all 16,164 feasible and plausible regression models, and identify those structural factors which are
consistently associated with immigrant segregation across these models. Our findings advance
the understanding of how segregation is connected to local and national structural conditions and
stimulates re-thinking existing theories about the emergence and consequences of segregation. We
also provide a public dataset containing all segregation measures and macro-level indicators. This
resource enables researchers, policymakers, and urban planners to explore and re-use our results
for further research.

2 Patterns of Segregation across Europe
In our main results, we assess segregation with the spatial dissimilarity index eDas proposed by
Reardon et al. (2008). It measures ‘how different the composition of the individuals’ local en-
vironments are, on average, from the composition of the population [in the FUA] as a whole’
(Reardon et al., 2008, see Methods section for more details); in other words, how unevenly im-
migrants and natives are distributed across space. We define the local environment with a 1km
radius, which approximates institutional neighbourhoods within which most individuals can reach
essential amenities (Reardon et al., 2008). We begin with the comparison of segregation levels
(research question 1) and then analyse the correlates of segregation (research question 2).
Mapping Segregation Levels Across Europe. To illustrate our measure of segregation, Figures
1 A) and B) depict the variation of the immigrant share per 1×1 km grid cell for the two FUAs
of Leicester (United Kingdom) and Bonn (Germany). In Leicester, the proportion of immigrants
varies widely across grid cells. Those grid cells with high proportions of immigrants are spatially
clustered around the urban core, while natives are overrepresented in the suburban surroundings,
indicating substantial segregation. This is reflected in Leicester’s dissimilarity index of 0.41 – one
of the highest in Europe. In Bonn, by contrast, the proportion of immigrants varies less across grid
cells, and grid cells with high proportions of immigrants are distributed across the entire FUA,
including its suburban areas. Correspondingly, the spatial dissimilarity index for Bonn is 0.17, and
thus significantly lower than in Leicester. See supplementary Figure A1 for additional examples.
Figure 1 C) maps the spatial dissimilarity index eDacross all 717 FUAs, revealing that segrega-
tion is stronger in Western and Northern vis-` a-vis Eastern and Southern Europe (see also Figure
2 A). The FUAs with the highest levels of residential segregation are primarily located in the
United Kingdom, northern France, and Belgium. Segregation is also substantial in the Nether-
lands, Germany (particularly East Germany), Denmark, Poland, Sweden, and Finland. FUAs in
most Eastern and Southern European countries are considerably less segregated. There are, how-
ever, two notable exceptions: Norwegian FUAs are less segregated than those in other Northern
European countries, and Polish FUAs are more segregated than those in other Eastern European
countries.
Comparing Patterns of Segregation across Europe. Figure 2 C) summarizes the distribution of
these segregation indices in a boxplot for each country, with dots representing individual FUAs and
capitals highlighted in black. Countries are ordered by their median segregation level, mirroring
the Western/Northern vs. Eastern/Southern gradient in segregation (see also Figure 1 C and 2
A). Roughly 40% of the total variation in segregation occurs between and 60% within countries,
suggesting that both country- and urban-level characteristics are relevant for segregation. Within-
country variation is particularly visible in the five most populous countries (Germany, France,
United Kingdom, Italy, Spain), where the gap between the most and the least segregated FUA
exceeds 0.2 scale points, i.e., half of its entire range. The variation is strongest in England, where
the dissimilarity index ranges from 0.09 in Stevenage to 0.43 in Leicester. Segregation ranges from
0.13 (Cannes-Antibes) to 0.40 (Amiens) in France, and from 0.10 (Konstanz) to 0.35 (Schweinfurt)
in Germany. Variation is smaller in Spain and Italy, where we measure segregation levels from 0.07

Most capitals (Figure 1 D) show higher segregation levels than their respective national average.
Large immigrant destinations in Western and Northern Europe, like Brussels (0.41), Amsterdam
(0.31), London (0.30), and Stockholm (0.28), have higher segregation levels than most other capi-
tals. The least segregated capitals at the 1km scale can be found in Eastern and Sourthern Europe:

Paris (France, 0.20), Berlin (Germany, 0.25), and other capitals fall in between. The full set of

capitals and their segregation levels are shown in Figure 1 C.
Across most urban areas, non-EU immigrants live more segregated than EU immigrants (see
Figure S2 A). Locations close to the EU border (such as Chelm or Zamo´ s´ c) are exceptional in
this aspect, as non-EU immigrants might be relatively close to the native population in terms
of language and cultural heritage in these places. Segregation indices of FUAs closer to the EU
borders (like Larisa, Trikala, or Siedlce) are also more affected by outlier grid cells that likely
contain facilities for asylum seekers. Nevertheless, the general impact of such outliers is very small
(see Figure S2 B).
Dimensions of Segregation. As shown by previous research, segregation is a multidimensional
phenomenon (Lichter et al., 2015; Massey and Denton, 1988; Reardon et al., 2008; Reardon and
O’Sullivan, 2004; R ¨uttenauer, 2022; Spierenburg et al., 2023). For instance, besides unevenness
(captured with the dissimilarity index eD), another dimension of segregation is immigrants’ isolation
from natives ( eP). Figure 2 B plots these dimensions against each other (see also Figure S7). For
most FUAs, immigrant isolation is lower than dissimilarity, as indicated by their location above
the 45 degree line. In particular, many Eastern European FUAs score high on spatial dissimilarity
but low on isolation (e.g. Zamo´ s´ c or P lock). This reflects the relatively low number of immigrants
living in these urban areas and the strong dependency of the isolation index on the immigrant
population. In fact, the size of the immigrant population explains 96% of the variation in eP. Net
of immigrant population, however, the isolation index ePis strongly correlated with eD(r = 0.79).
In line with previous research (Lichter et al., 2015; Reardon et al., 2008), segregation indices
decline when measured at larger spatial scales (e.g., 2km or 5km see Figure S3, panel A). Although
the overall regional pattern is unaffected (see Figures S5 and S6) and segregation levels generally
are highly correlated across spatial scales (e.g., r = 0.87 for 1km and 5km), there is interesting
geographical variation in the scale dependency of segregation levels. Specifically, several urban
areas in Eastern and Southern European countries are much less segregated at larger spatial scales
as compared to the 1km level (see Figure S8). Many urban areas in Western and Northern Europe,
on the other hand, exhibit high levels of segregation even at broader spatial scales.
Rather than the spatial scale itself, a key driver of segregation in Western European FUAs is
the stark contrast in diversity between urban cores and their surrounding suburban zones. When
comparing dissimilarity indices for entire FUAs with those calculated for core cities only (see
Figure S3, panel B), we find that most cities are less segregated within the urban core than across
the whole commuting zone. Examples include some of the most strongly segregated capitals: for
instance, the spatial dissimilarity index for the Brussels urban area is 0.41, while its core city only
exhibits a dissimilarity index of 0.15. Likewise, Amsterdam has an overall dissimilarity of 0.31,
while its core city only exhibits a value of 0.12. This urban–suburban divide closely mirrors findings
from the US context (Elbers, 2024; Lichter et al., 2015; Logan et al., 2023; Logan and Parman,
2025), suggesting that large-scale segregation between inner cities and suburban commuting zones
characterises North American and European metropolitan regions.

3 Urban- and Country-Level Correlates of Segregation
We next examine which characteristics of urban areas are systematically linked to segregation using
our core measure: the spatial dissimilarity index with a 1km radius. Since we consider a wide range
of potentially interrelated characteristics, we do not estimate a single ‘most likely’ omnibus model
for these associations. Instead, we borrow from the logic of specification curve analysis (SCA),
estimating all plausible and feasible model specifications to determine which associations are robust
across these specifications (Simonsohn et al., 2020). In total, we estimate 9,990 model specifications
which all include five FUA population controls (population size, density, concentration, immigrant
proportion, and educational composition), up to four varying additional FUA-level correlates, and
country fixed effects. For each correlate of segregation, this yields a distribution of coefficients.
Three increasingly conservative tests assess the robustness of associations across specifications (see
Methods section for more information).
Figure 3 illustrates this approach for the association between segregation and population dis-
persion, which captures how spatially dispersed the overall population is across the FUA. The
bivariate association in panel A suggests that stronger population dispersion is linked to higher
levels of segregation. Panel B displays the distribution of estimated associations across all specifi-
cations from the SCA, which differ in the set of covariates included next to population dispersion.
Test 1 evaluates whether at least 95% of all specifications predict the same sign for the variable’s
association with segregation. Tests 2-3 further compare the observed distribution of estimates
with 500 counterfactual bootstrapped distributions that enforce a null association between the
8

focal variable and segregation (Simonsohn et al., 2020). Next to the observed coefficients in grey,
panel C illustrates ten example counterfactual distributions. Test 2 assesses whether the median
observed estimate is larger than the median in at least 95% of the 500 bootstrapped distributions.
Panel D visualizes the results of test 3, which considers each model specification separately and
ranks the estimates across specifications by size. For each specification, we test if the observed
estimate falls outside of the 95% quantile band of ranked counterfactual bootstrapped estimates
(dashed lines), indicating that the observed estimate will almost never be induced if there is no
actual association. An association passes this test if observed estimates fall outside of the quantile
band for at least 95% of all specifications. As this third test is very conservative, we also label
associations as robust that only pass tests 1 and 2 but not test 3.
The association between population dispersion and segregation in Figure 3 passes all three tests.
This provides robust support for the idea that segregation of immigrants is stronger in FUAs whose
population is distributed more evenly across the entire urban area. When most of the population
lives very concentrated in only a few parts of the city, immigrant segregation is lower. Figure
4 extends this example to the complete set of covariates, grouped into five thematic domains:
population characteristics (A), economic conditions (B), the housing market (C), migration flow
and immigrant composition (D), and country-level characteristics (E). Except for the country-level
characteristics, associations are estimated using models with country fixed effects, i.e., models that
only consider variation within rather than across countries.
Panel A: Population characteristics. Next to higher population dispersion, also lower popu-
lation density is robustly associated with higher levels of segregation across all statistical tests.
Furthermore, FUAs with larger populations are more segregated in all specifications, though the
robustness of this link does not extend to our most conservative statistical test. Regarding popu-
lation demographics, a higher proportion of immigrants is associated with lower segregation, but
effect sizes vary widely across specifications. All tests further support that a larger proportion of
highly educated residents and a smaller group of right-wing voters correlate with lower levels of
segregation.
Panel B: Economic conditions. Favourable economic conditions, i.e., higher GDP per capita,
lower poverty risk, and lower unemployment rate, are all linked to lower segregation levels, but
only poverty risk is robustly associated across all statistical tests. Immigrant segregation is also
consistently higher in FUAs with greater economic inequality and in FUAs where immigrants’
unemployment rates exceed natives’ more strongly. Somewhat surprisingly, segregation levels are
also higher in urban areas where the occupational status of employed immigrants is more similar to
that of natives, i.e., immigrant-native inequality is smaller. The size of the agricultural, industrial,
and service sectors is not consistently related to segregation.

Figure 4: Specification Curve Analysis of associations of levels of segregation with (A) FUA pop-
ulation characteristics, (B) FUA economic conditions, (C) FUA housing market conditions, (D)
FUA immigration flow and composition, (E) country-level characteristics. Note: The universe
of ‘reasonable’ model specifications excludes specifications including multiple covariates from the
same covariate subgroup. For example, we do not estimate models that include both GDP per
capita and unemployment rate, two indicators in the economic performance covariate subgroup.

Panel C: Housing market. Conditions in local housing markets are also systematically related
to segregation. FUAs with high apartment prices consistently have lower levels of segregation,
while a higher proportion of households overburdened with housing expenses (>40% of income)
is not systematically linked to segregation. A higher proportion of homeowners and of households
that have lived in the same residence the year before are linked to lower segregation. This is
consistent with the inhibition of segregation processes by low housing turnover. Tighter housing
markets – characterized by fewer dwellings per resident and a higher occupancy rate – are also
robustly associated with higher segregation levels. More recently built housing has a weak positive
association with segregation, but does not pass our more conservative robustness tests.
Panel D: Flow and composition of immigrant population. Segregation is higher in FUAs with
larger recent inflows of immigrants, but these associations are robust only when considering inflows
from the previous year rather than longer time horizons. This indicates higher levels of segregation
in popular international migration-destination hubs. Concerning the composition of the immigrant
population by origin, we find no robust link between segregation and the proportion of immigrants
from MENA or Latin American countries. However, segregation is consistently higher in FUAs
with a lower proportion of EU and other ‘Western’ immigrants, a higher proportion of immigrants
from Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia, and a higher proportion from lower- and lower-middle-income
countries.
Panel E: Country characteristics. Finally, to study links between country characteristics and
segregation, we switch from models with country fixed effects to random-intercept multilevel SCAs.
We retain the five basic FUA controls, up to four additional FUA covariates, and up to three
country-level covariates, for a total of 6,174 model specifications. We focus on indicators of policy
and migration history, which operate at the country rather than the urban area level. Panel
E of Figure 4 finds that neither levels of social expenditure nor the migration and immigrant
integration policies captured by the MIPEX index are consistently linked to segregation levels.
By contrast, housing policy is associated with segregation: segregation is higher in countries with
higher social housing expenditure and a higher proportion of the population receiving housing
allowances. However, we do not have data on the degree to which the social housing sector
is integrated into or separated from the private housing market. This may crucially shape the
impact of social housing on segregation. Finally, segregation is higher in established migration
destinations, i.e., countries in which the proportion of immigrants among the total population
exceeded 10% already in 2000. Table 1 summarizes the results of the specification curve analysis.
Other dimensions and measures of segregation. Our findings are remarkably consistent across
several alternative operationalisations of segregation (Figures S9, S10, S11). When capturing
segregation with the isolation rather than the dissimilarity index, associations remain qualitatively
similar: the direction of associations and the results of the statistical tests do not change; only the
share of Sub-Saharan immigrants and social housing expenditure are no longer robustly associated
with segregation. However, most coefficients shrink considerably in size due to the extraordinarily
strong dependence of the isolation index on the share of immigrants in the local population (Figure
S9 and Methods section).

Most associations also persist when measuring segregation at the 5km instead of the 1km scale
(Figure S10). The only notable change is that, at a larger spatial scale, educational composition
is no longer related to segregation. This may indicate that highly educated residents are more
likely to live in mixed neighbourhoods (e.g., in the city centre), but there is no association with
mixing across urban and suburban parts. Associations also persist when we focus on non-EU
immigrants rather than all immigrants (Figure S11), though the link between country-level social
housing expenditure disappears and the MIPEX score becomes more robustly positively linked to
segregation. In three additional robustness checks, we examine whether results change when we
exclude FUAs with fewer than 100,000 residents (Figure S12), FUAs with an immigrant population
of less than 5% (Figure S13), and FUAs next to national borders (Figure S14). Overall patterns
are very similar to the main analysis. However, a recurring observation across robustness checks is
that not all indicators of housing market tightness and turnover are as clearly linked to segregation
as in the main analysis, although substantive insights remain unchanged. At the country level,
social housing expenditure proves to be least robustly associated with segregation across these
additional analyses.
4 Discussion
This study provides the most comprehensive assessment of immigrant-native residential segregation
across Europe, covering all 717 Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) in 30 countries. Our findings reveal
12

that segregation is higher in Western and Northern Europe vis-` a-vis large parts of Eastern and
Southern Europe. However, 60% of the variation in segregation levels occurs within countries. We
find that segregation is systematically linked to urban area population characteristics, economy,
housing market, immigrant inflow and composition. At the country level, segregation is linked to
migration histories and housing policies, but unrelated to migration policy.
Our study makes two key contributions. First, the results expand, update, and systematize
our knowledge of immigrant-native segregation across Europe. Our study provides harmonised,
high-resolution segregation estimates for all urban areas in 30 European countries. While such
large-scale comparisons of segregation levels across urban areas have been carried out in the US
(Iceland and Scopilliti, 2008; Lichter et al., 2024, 2015; Parisi et al., 2025; Reardon et al., 2008),
equivalent evidence in Europe has so far been missing. We show that immigrant-native segregation
is highly uneven across Europe, with a clear North/West vs. South/East divide – although Poland’s
high levels of unevenness are somewhat outstanding. Moreover, non-EU immigrants are typically
more segregated than their EU counterparts, with urban areas near EU borders representing a
notable exception. We also show that segregation in European urban areas is strongly shaped by
large-scale patterns, with diverse urban cores contrasting sharply with the underrepresentation of
immigrant minorities in suburban areas and commuting zones.
Second, we examine a broad set of urban and national characteristics as potential correlates
of segregation. As summarised in Table 1, segregation is consistently higher in urban areas with
larger populations and greater spatial dispersion of the population, but lower in urban areas with
high population density and larger immigrant populations. Segregation is also lower in urban
areas with a more educated population, fewer right-wing voters, higher economic performance,
and lower economic inequality. Associations with economic immigrant-native inequality are less
consistent: disproportionately high unemployment rates among immigrants are related to higher
segregation, but a relatively higher occupational status of immigrants is also related to higher,
not lower segregation. More housing-turnover and greater tightness of the housing market are
linked to higher segregation – as are immigrant populations from lower-income countries, Sub-
Saharan Africa, and Asia, rather than from the EU or other ‘Western’ countries. International
immigration hubs that have recently attracted many immigrants are more segregated. Across
countries, however, more established immigrant destinations are more segregated, indicating a
local consolidation of immigrant groups in these contexts. Segregation is also stronger in countries
with greater social housing expenditure and greater uptake of housing allowances, while migration
and integration policies are not connected to segregation levels.
Several findings align with long-standing theoretical expectations of segregation. For example,
the link between higher housing-turnover and greater segregation is consistent with Schelling’s
(1978) segregation model, which posits that segregation emerges through repeated residential
moves. Similarly, our findings align with place stratification theory (Logan and Alba, 1993),
highlighting the role of discrimination: segregation is higher in areas with stronger support for far-
right parties and in cities with larger shares of stigmatised origin-groups. While overall economic
inequality is linked to higher segregation, our findings on native–immigrant inequality are more
13

nuanced than previous findings (Fossett, 2011; Iceland and Wilkes, 2006): segregation is higher
when unemployment gaps are larger, but also when occupational differences among the employed
are smaller – supporting spatial assimilation theory in the first case, and yet contradicting it in the
second. Finally, higher segregation levels in major immigration destinations and countries with
a long-standing immigration legacy underscore the role of ethnic enclaves and path-dependent
settlement patterns (even more so for non-EU immigrants).
At the same time, we identify systematic links between segregation levels and structural char-
acteristics that segregation theories remain largely silent about. We find that dispersed settlement
structures facilitate separation, highlighting the role of metropolitan morphology as a macro-spatial
feature of segregation. Higher education levels are associated with more mixing on the small-scale
neighbourhood level, but not at the macro scale between urban cores and suburban surroundings.
FUAs with higher apartment prices exhibit lower segregation levels, possibly because high housing
costs constrain households’ ability to act on discriminatory preferences, forcing them to prioritize
affordability over selective location choices (Logan and Alba, 1993). This interpretation is fur-
ther supported by our finding that high housing prices reduce segregation more among non-EU
immigrants, toward whom exclusionary preferences may be more pronounced. Concerning policy,
earlier studies have suggested that countries with multiculturalist approaches exhibit lower levels
of segregation (Koopmans, 2010). However, drawing on a larger and more comprehensive cross-
country dataset than previous research, the association between migration policy and segregation
does not appear robust. We instead find that higher social housing expenditure and greater uptake
of housing allowances are linked to higher levels of segregation. However, social housing systems
differ substantially in their design – some are closely integrated with the private housing market,
while others are more separated – shaping the extent to which these policies influence residential
segregation (Andersson et al., 2018; Marci´ nczak et al., 2023).
We acknowledge three main limitations of the present study. First, a drawback of our broad
geographical scope and the harmonised data is that information on the immigrant population is less
granular. Accordingly, we cannot differentiate immigrants by country of origin, length of residence,
or socio-economic status. We also cannot compare the residential patterns of immigrants to those of
their descendants across Europe. However, a robustness check (Figure S15) with more detailed data
from the Netherlands shows a strong correlation (r = 0.9) of segregation levels among immigrants
and their descendants. Still, documenting the variation across generations can be important for
understanding long-term integration trajectories.
Second, while the 1×1 km grid resolution of the census data ensures comparability across
Europe, it does not capture geographical sorting at smaller spatial scales, such as residential blocks
or streets. Such micro-level segregation within census grid cells may be particularly pronounced in
densely populated urban areas. At the same time, the neighbourhood within 1km reach seems to
be important for many aspects of social integration, such as day-to-day interaction, local amenities,
and school catchment areas (Reardon and O’Sullivan, 2004).
Third, our analysis of the structural correlates of segregation is observational and cannot iden-
tify causal effects. Patterns of segregation emerge over time through complex interactions be-
14

tween individual residential choices, institutional practices, and urban development (Desmond and
Wilmers, 2019; Elbers, 2024; Krysan and Crowder, 2017; Logan, 2012; Logan and Alba, 1993).
Some of the correlates we have considered, such as local inequality between natives and immi-
grants, can not only be a precursor, but also a consequence of segregation. Instead of a causal
assessment, the Specification Curve Analysis provides a rich descriptive overview of the correlates
of segregation, accounting for a comprehensive set of potential covariates.
Nevertheless, our documentation of segregation across Europe and the analysis of its macro-
level correlates offers several opportunities for future research. First, our harmonised segregation
indices can serve as a valuable resource for researchers who need to strategically select urban
areas for in-depth studies, such as qualitative or longitudinal approaches. Such studies can explore
how local institutions, histories, and policies interact to shape segregation dynamics over time
(Bruch and Swait, 2019). Second, our comprehensive analysis of the correlates of segregation
provides a starting point for future causal research investigating whether the associations persist
in longitudinal designs and how immigrant-native segregation co-evolves with other dimensions of
segregation, such as socio-economic segregation (Ubareviˇ cien˙ e et al., 2025). As such, our findings
provide a foundation for refining and expanding theoretical frameworks on the contextual drivers
of segregation. Finally, our documentation of substantial variation in segregation levels across and
within countries raises the question of whether differences in local segregation levels translate into
diverging lived experiences among immigrants and whether they are mirrored in their integration
outcomes. Accordingly, our findings also call for further research on the consequences of residential
segregation.

Methods
Data
Functional Urban Areas. To identify urban areas across Europe, we rely on the joint Euro-
stat/OECD classification of Functional Urban Areas (FUAs). Each FUA consists of an urban
centre/city and its commuting zone, i.e., all surrounding areas in which at least 15% of the popula-
tion commute to the urban centre (for details, see Eurostat, 2025b). This uniform way of identifying
urban areas across all 30 countries avoids measurement issues arising from country-specific vari-
ations in administrative definitions of urban areas and has become standard in the comparative
European literature on segregation (Marci´ nczak et al., 2023; Benassi et al., 2020). The definition
of the FUAs also closely resembles the definition of metropolitan areas usually used in the US
segregation literature (Lichter et al., 2015; Reardon et al., 2008). We use shapefile information on
the geographical boundaries of FUAs provided by Eurostat.
Local native and immigrant population. To identify the spatial distribution of the local native
and immigrant population, we rely on data from the 2021/2022 censuses conducted in all 30
countries. For all countries but the UK, Eurostat provides aggregated and harmonized data. For
all 1×1 km grid cells, these data capture the number of residents born in the country of residence,
in another EU country, and in a non-EU country (Eurostat, 2025a). For the United Kingdom,
we harmonised data from three separate sources: The 2021 census for England and Wales, the
2022 census for Scotland, and the 2021 census for Northern Ireland. While the latter is available
in a 1×1 km grid cell format directly comparable to the remaining European data, the other two
sources provide the relevant information at the spatial resolution of Lower Statistical Output Areas
(LSOA, 1,400 inhabitants on average). We performed dasymetric mapping techniques to translate
those into a 1×1 km regular grid. Intuitively, we first used the data from the input layer and
distribute the characteristics of each LSOA’s along a 100m resolution population layer. In this
step, the population characteristics are distributed to match the the number of residents along the
100m resolution population layer. Subsequently, we interpolated from this 100m layer to the final
1×1 km grid. This provides us with a harmonized set of 1×1 km grid cells and their composition
in terms of natives and immigrants across all 30 countries.
FUA and country-level correlates of segregation. To examine the correlates of residential
segregation, we collect FUA- and country-level information from Eurostat, the OECD, the UN,
the European Election Database, and the Migrant Integration Policy Database. Missing values were
imputed using multivariate imputation by chained equations with 20 imputed datasets (Buuren
and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011). For each variable, Table S1 in the Supplementary Material lists
the definition, the spatial level of measurement, and the year of measurement.

Statistical Methods
To investigate which FUA- and country characteristics are robustly associated with residential seg-
regation, we use specification curve analysis for inference with non-experimental data (Simonsohn
et al., 2020). We first define the universe of feasible specifications that are also plausible (Auspurg,
2025).
17

For all urban area-level analysis, we run regression models with country fixed effects. All mod-
els include basic population controls (population size, population density, population dispersion,
percentage of immigrants, educational composition). In addition, they contain a set of one to
four additional FUA-level variables. These sets include all possible specifications, excluding those
combinations with multiple variables from within the same variable subgroup. For instance, both
GDP per capita and the unemployment rate capture economic performance, so they are not in-
cluded in the same model. Table S1 in Supplementary Material provides an overview of all variable
subgroups and the combinations of variables that are (not) estimated in the same model. These
criteria result in a total of 9,990 fixed-effects models for the urban area-level covariates.
For the analysis of country-level characteristics, we use random-effects multilevel models with
random intercepts. Next to FUA-level population controls and up to four additional FUA char-
acteristics, we include up to three country-level characteristics in these models. This results in a
total of 6,174 random-effects multilevel models.

structure.title: Immigrant Residential Segregation in Europe: A Comparative Study of Spatial Segregation Patterns in Urban Areas across 30 Countries
structure.summary: This partial document describes a comparative study on immigrant residential segregation across urban areas in 30 European countries. The study aims to understand how segregation varies geographically and which urban and country-level factors are associated with these patterns. It utilizes harmonized 1x1 km grid-level census data to calculate Dissimilarity Indices for 717 Functional Urban Areas. The research combines this data with information on demographics, economy, housing, immigrant populations, and policy, employing a Specification Curve Analysis across numerous regression models to identify robust correlates of segregation. Key findings indicate higher segregation in Western and Northern Europe, driven by macro-spatial dynamics between urban cores and suburbs. Segregation is linked to local population composition and distribution, economic conditions, housing markets, and immigrant population characteristics. At the national level, established immigrant destinations show higher segregation, while migration and integration policies do not have a consistent link. The study provides a comprehensive assessment of immigrant segregation in Europe and its relationship to spatial integration.

nodes.title: Introduction and Background
nodes.summary: This partial document introduces the topic of residential segregation, highlighting its significant negative implications for minority groups and social cohesion. It reviews existing research on racial segregation in the US and immigrant segregation in Europe, outlining the traditional causes: in-group preferences, socio-economic disparities, and housing market discrimination. The document then points out limitations in previous comparative European studies, such as limited country coverage, outdated data, and inconsistent definitions. To address these, the authors present a comprehensive analysis of immigrant residential segregation across 717 Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) in 30 European countries using recent census data. They aim to understand the variation in segregation levels and identify associated urban and national characteristics. The study links segregation indices to a rich dataset of FUA and country-level indicators and employs Specification Curve Analysis to identify consistently associated structural factors. The document also mentions a public dataset of segregation measures and indicators for future research and policy use, and includes a figure illustrating spatial distributions of immigrant populations and segregation indices.

nodes.title: Patterns of Segregation across Europe
nodes.summary:
This partial document focuses on analyzing patterns of residential segregation across Europe, specifically examining the distribution of immigrants and natives within urban areas. The main points covered are:

*   **Measurement of Segregation:** The document utilizes the spatial dissimilarity index ($e_D$) proposed by Reardon et al. (2008) to measure how unevenly immigrants and natives are distributed across space within a 1km radius local environment.
*   **Mapping Segregation Levels:** It illustrates segregation levels with examples from Leicester (UK) and Bonn (Germany), highlighting significant differences in immigrant distribution and corresponding dissimilarity indices. A map of $e_D$ across 717 Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) reveals stronger segregation in Western and Northern Europe compared to Eastern and Southern Europe.
*   **Geographical Patterns:** The document identifies FUAs with the highest segregation in the UK, northern France, and Belgium, with substantial segregation also present in the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, Poland, Sweden, and Finland. Eastern and Southern European countries generally show lower segregation, with notable exceptions like Norway and Poland.
*   **Within-Country Variation:** It highlights that a significant portion of segregation variation occurs within countries, particularly in populous nations like Germany, France, the UK, Italy, and Spain, where the gap between the most and least segregated FUAs is substantial.
*   **Capital City Segregation:** Most capital cities exhibit higher segregation levels than their national averages, with large immigrant destinations like Brussels, Amsterdam, London, and Stockholm showing particularly high levels. Least segregated capitals are found in Eastern and Southern Europe.
*   **EU vs. Non-EU Immigrant Segregation:** Generally, non-EU immigrants live more segregated than EU immigrants, with exceptions noted near EU borders or in areas with facilities for asylum seekers.
*   **Dimensions of Segregation:** The document briefly touches upon segregation as a multidimensional phenomenon, mentioning isolation ($e_P$) as another dimension and noting its strong correlation with population size and dissimilarity.
*   **Scale Dependency:** Segregation indices decrease at larger spatial scales, but the overall regional patterns remain largely consistent. However, urban areas in Eastern and Southern Europe show greater reduction in segregation at larger scales compared to Western and Northern Europe.
*   **Urban-Suburban Divide:** A key driver of segregation in Western Europe is the contrast between urban cores and surrounding suburban zones, with segregation being higher across the entire commuting zone than within the core city itself, mirroring findings from the US.
*   **Correlates of Segregation:** The document introduces an analysis of urban and country-level correlates of segregation using Specification Curve Analysis (SCA) to identify robust associations across various model specifications. An example is provided for the association between segregation and population dispersion.

nodes.title: Urban- and Country-Level Correlates of Segregation
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a study investigating the correlates of immigrant-native residential segregation across European Functional Urban Areas (FUAs). The main points covered are:

*   **Methodology:** The study employs Specification Curve Analysis (SCA) to assess the robustness of associations between various urban and country-level characteristics and segregation. This involves estimating a large number of model specifications with different covariate combinations and then testing the consistency of the results across these specifications. Three increasingly conservative tests are used to determine robustness.
*   **Example Analysis (Population Dispersion):** Figure 3 illustrates the SCA approach using the association between segregation and population dispersion. It shows how bivariate associations are compared with distributions of coefficients from SCA and counterfactual null distributions to assess robustness.
*   **Urban-Level Correlates of Segregation:** The document details findings for several categories of urban-level characteristics:
    *   **Population Characteristics:** Higher population dispersion, lower population density, larger population size, a higher proportion of highly educated residents, and a smaller proportion of right-wing voters are associated with lower segregation. A higher proportion of immigrants is associated with lower segregation, but with varying effect sizes.
    *   **Economic Conditions:** Favorable economic conditions (higher GDP per capita, lower poverty risk, lower unemployment) are linked to lower segregation, with poverty risk being robust. Higher economic inequality and greater immigrant unemployment relative to natives are linked to higher segregation.
    *   **Housing Market:** High apartment prices, a higher proportion of homeowners, and a higher proportion of long-term residents are linked to lower segregation. Tighter housing markets (fewer dwellings per resident, higher occupancy) are robustly associated with higher segregation.
    *   **Migration Flow and Composition:** Higher recent immigrant inflows are linked to higher segregation, but this is only robust for inflows from the previous year. Segregation is higher in FUAs with a lower proportion of EU/Western immigrants and a higher proportion of immigrants from Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and lower-income countries.
*   **Country-Level Correlates of Segregation:** Using random-intercept multilevel SCAs, the study examines country-level characteristics. Social housing expenditure and a higher proportion of the population receiving housing allowances are associated with higher segregation. Segregation is also higher in established migration destination countries. Social expenditure and migration policies (MIPEX) are not consistently linked to segregation.
*   **Robustness Checks:** The document discusses findings from several robustness checks, including using alternative segregation measures (isolation index), different spatial scales (5km radius), focusing on non-EU immigrants, and excluding FUAs based on population size, immigrant proportion, or proximity to national borders. Overall patterns remain consistent, though some specific associations show varying degrees of robustness across these checks.

nodes.title: Discussion
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on the relationship between various urban area, country, and migrant characteristics and immigrant-native residential segregation. It presents a table summarizing these associations, categorizing them as negative, none, or positive. The text then discusses the robustness of these findings across different spatial scales (1km vs. 5km), immigrant groups (all vs. non-EU), and through additional robustness checks excluding certain types of Functional Urban Areas (FUAs). Key points include:

*   **Factors associated with segregation:** The table outlines specific urban population characteristics (density, % immigrants, education, dispersion, size, far-right voters), economic factors (performance, immigrant unemployment, sectoral composition, occupational status), housing market dynamics (residence stability, homeownership, housing stock recency, market tightness, affordability), migrant flow/composition (origin countries, recent inflow), and country-level characteristics (social expenditure, migration policy, established destination status, social housing allowances) that are linked to segregation.
*   **Scale of analysis:** Segregation associations generally persist at a larger spatial scale (5km), with the notable exception of educational composition no longer being related to segregation, suggesting highly educated individuals might live in mixed neighborhoods within cities but not necessarily across urban/suburban divides.
*   **Immigrant group focus:** Associations remain similar when focusing on non-EU immigrants, although the link between country-level social housing expenditure weakens, and migration policy indicators (MIPEX) become more strongly associated with segregation.
*   **Robustness checks:** Excluding smaller FUAs, FUAs with low immigrant populations, or FUAs near national borders generally yields similar patterns. However, housing market indicators show less consistent links to segregation in these checks, and social housing expenditure is the least robust country-level association.
*   **Study scope:** The study is presented as a comprehensive assessment of immigrant-native residential segregation across Europe, covering a large number of Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) in 30 countries.

nodes.title: Key Contributions and Findings
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses immigrant-native segregation across Europe, highlighting its uneven distribution with a North/West vs. South/East divide. It emphasizes that while regional differences exist, a significant portion of segregation variation occurs within countries. The study identifies several key factors influencing segregation at both the urban and national levels.

At the urban level, segregation is linked to population characteristics (larger populations, greater dispersion, lower density), economic factors (higher economic performance, lower inequality), housing market dynamics (higher turnover, tighter markets), and immigrant inflow and composition (origin countries, recent immigration hubs). It also notes that segregation is lower in urban areas with more educated populations and fewer right-wing voters.

At the country level, segregation is associated with migration histories and housing policies, but not migration policy. The document also points out that non-EU immigrants tend to be more segregated than EU counterparts, with exceptions near EU borders. It further suggests that established immigrant destinations experience higher segregation, indicating local consolidation.

The study's contributions include providing harmonized, high-resolution segregation estimates for European urban areas, filling a gap in large-scale comparative research. It also examines a broad range of urban and national characteristics as correlates of segregation, finding that some results align with established theories like Schelling's segregation model and place stratification theory.

nodes.title: Alignment with and Divergence from Existing Theories
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses immigrant-native segregation across Europe, highlighting key findings and contributions of a study. The main points covered are:

*   **Geographical Variation:** Segregation is generally higher in Western and Northern Europe compared to Eastern and Southern Europe, though a significant portion of variation occurs within countries.
*   **Correlates of Segregation:** Segregation is linked to various urban and national characteristics, including:
    *   **Urban Area Characteristics:** Larger population, spatial dispersion, population density, immigrant population size, education levels, political leanings (fewer right-wing voters), economic performance, economic inequality, housing market dynamics (turnover, tightness), and immigrant origin countries.
    *   **Country-Level Characteristics:** Migration histories and housing policies, but not migration policy itself.
*   **Key Contributions of the Study:**
    *   **Systematized Knowledge:** Provides harmonized, high-resolution segregation estimates for urban areas across 30 European countries, filling a gap in large-scale European comparisons.
    *   **Uneven Distribution:** Demonstrates highly uneven segregation across Europe with a North/West vs. South/East divide, noting Poland as an exception. Non-EU immigrants are typically more segregated than EU counterparts.
    *   **Macro-Scale Patterns:** Segregation is shaped by large-scale patterns, with diverse urban cores contrasting with immigrant underrepresentation in suburban areas.
*   **Theoretical Alignment and Novel Findings:**
    *   **Alignment:** Findings align with theories like Schelling's segregation model (housing turnover), place stratification theory (discrimination, far-right support), and ethnic enclave/path-dependent settlement patterns.
    *   **Novelty:** Identifies links to structural characteristics not fully explained by existing theories, such as metropolitan morphology, higher education levels (at neighborhood scale), and the role of high apartment prices in reducing segregation by prioritizing affordability.
*   **Policy Implications:** While multiculturalist approaches were previously thought to reduce segregation, the study finds no robust association between migration policy and segregation. Instead, social housing expenditure and housing allowance uptake are linked to higher segregation, though the design of social housing systems is a crucial factor.
*   **Limitations:** The study acknowledges limitations including less granular data on immigrant populations (inability to differentiate by origin, residence length, or socio-economic status), the inability to compare immigrants with their descendants, and the resolution of data (1x1 km grid) which may miss micro-level segregation. The analysis is also observational, preventing causal inference.

nodes.title: Limitations of the Study
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses findings on residential segregation, particularly concerning immigrants. It highlights that segregation is influenced by unemployment gaps and occupational differences among the employed, with implications for spatial assimilation theory. The text also points to the role of ethnic enclaves and settlement patterns in major immigration destinations.

The document identifies links between segregation and structural characteristics not typically addressed by segregation theories, such as metropolitan morphology and housing prices. It suggests that higher apartment prices may reduce segregation by limiting households' ability to act on discriminatory preferences.

Regarding policy, the study finds that multiculturalist approaches do not robustly correlate with lower segregation. Instead, higher social housing expenditure and housing allowance uptake are linked to increased segregation, though the design of social housing systems plays a crucial role.

The document acknowledges three main limitations: the lack of granular data on immigrant populations (preventing differentiation by origin, residence length, or socio-economic status), the inability to capture micro-level segregation within census grid cells, and the observational nature of the analysis, which prevents causal inference.

Despite these limitations, the study offers opportunities for future research, including the use of harmonized segregation indices for selecting urban areas for in-depth studies, further causal research on the correlates of segregation, and investigations into the consequences of residential segregation on immigrants' lived experiences and integration outcomes.

nodes.title: Spatial Dissimilarity Index (eD)
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the methodology used to measure residential segregation. It focuses on two key spatial dissimilarity indices:

*   **Spatial Dissimilarity Index (eD):** This index measures the unevenness of immigrant-native composition across a Functional Urban Area (FUA). It accounts for geographic locality by interpolating population characteristics within a defined radius, weighting deviations from the FUA's mean composition by local population density. Higher values indicate greater segregation. The document highlights its scale-invariance and comparability across different urban areas. A radius of 1km is used for the main analysis, with supplementary results for other radii.

*   **Spatial Isolation Index (meP\*):** This index measures the extent to which immigrants are exposed to other immigrants rather than natives in their local environments. It quantifies the average proportion of immigrants within an immigrant's local environment and is dependent on the overall immigrant share in the urban area.

The document also briefly introduces the statistical method used for analysis: **specification curve analysis**, which is employed for inference with non-experimental data to identify robust associations between FUA and country characteristics and residential segregation.

The study identifies several key factors influencing segregation at both the urban and national levels.

At the urban level, segregation is linked to population characteristics (larger populations, greater dispersion, lower density), economic factors (higher economic performance, lower inequality), housing market dynamics (higher turnover, tighter markets), and immigrant inflow and composition (origin countries, recent immigration hubs). At the country level, segregation is associated with migration histories and housing policies, but not migration policy. The document also points out that non-EU immigrants tend to be more segregated than EU counterparts, with exceptions near EU borders. It further suggests that established immigrant destinations experience higher segregation, indicating local consolidation.

The study's contributions include providing harmonized, high-resolution segregation estimates for European urban areas, filling a gap in large-scale comparative research. It also examines a broad range of urban and national characteristics as correlates of segregation, finding that some results align with established theories like Schelling's segregation model and place stratification theory.

nodes.title: Theoretical Implications
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses immigrant-native segregation across Europe, highlighting key findings and contributions of a study. The main points covered are:

*   **Geographical Variation:** Segregation is generally higher in Western and Northern Europe compared to Eastern and Southern Europe, though a significant portion of variation occurs within countries.
*   **Correlates of Segregation:** Segregation is linked to various urban and national characteristics, including:
    *   **Urban Area Characteristics:** Larger population, spatial dispersion, population density, immigrant population size, education levels, political leanings (fewer right-wing voters), economic performance, economic inequality, housing market dynamics (turnover, tightness), and immigrant origin countries.
    *   **Country-Level Characteristics:** Migration histories and housing policies, but not migration policy itself.
*   **Key Contributions of the Study:**
    *   **Systematized Knowledge:** Provides harmonized, high-resolution segregation estimates for urban areas across 30 European countries, filling a gap in large-scale European comparisons.
    *   **Uneven Distribution:** Demonstrates highly uneven segregation across Europe with a North/West vs. South/East divide, noting Poland as an exception. Non-EU immigrants are typically more segregated than EU counterparts.
    *   **Macro-Scale Patterns:** Segregation is shaped by large-scale patterns, with diverse urban cores contrasting with immigrant underrepresentation in suburban areas.
*   **Theoretical Alignment and Novel Findings:**
    *   **Alignment:** Findings align with theories like Schelling's segregation model (housing turnover), place stratification theory (discrimination, far-right support), and ethnic enclave/path-dependent settlement patterns.
    *   **Novelty:** Identifies links to structural characteristics not fully explained by existing theories, such as metropolitan morphology, higher education levels (at neighborhood scale), and the role of high apartment prices in reducing segregation by prioritizing affordability.
*   **Policy Implications:** While multiculturalist approaches were previously thought to reduce segregation, the study finds no robust association between migration policy and segregation. Instead, social housing expenditure and housing allowance uptake are linked to higher segregation, though the design of social housing systems is a crucial factor.
*   **Limitations:** The study acknowledges limitations including less granular data on immigrant populations (inability to differentiate by origin, residence length, or socio-economic status), the inability to compare immigrants with their descendants, and the resolution of data (1x1 km grid) which may miss micro-level segregation. The analysis is also observational, preventing causal inference.

The document identifies links between segregation and structural characteristics not typically addressed by segregation theories, such as metropolitan morphology and housing prices. Regarding policy, the study finds that multiculturalist approaches do not robustly correlate with lower segregation. Instead, higher social housing expenditure and housing allowance uptake are linked to increased segregation, though the design of social housing systems plays a crucial role.

The document acknowledges three main limitations: the lack of granular data on immigrant populations (preventing differentiation by origin, residence length, or socio-economic status), the inability to capture micro-level segregation within census grid cells, and the observational nature of the analysis, which prevents causal inference.

Despite these limitations, the study offers opportunities for future research, including the use of harmonized segregation indices for selecting urban areas for in-depth studies, further causal research on the correlates of segregation, and investigations into the consequences of residential segregation on immigrants' lived experiences and integration outcomes.

nodes.title: Limitations and Future Research

This partial document focuses on the analysis of residential segregation in Europe, specifically concerning the spatial distribution of native and immigrant populations.

The main points covered are:

*   **Contextualizing Segregation:** It acknowledges the complex interplay between individual residential choices, institutional practices, and urban development in shaping segregation.
*   **Descriptive Analysis of Correlates:** The document emphasizes that its approach, Specification Curve Analysis, provides a rich descriptive overview of factors associated with segregation, rather than a purely causal assessment. It notes that some correlates, like local inequality between natives and immigrants, can be both a precursor and a consequence of segregation.
*   **Opportunities for Future Research:** The document highlights several avenues for future research stemming from its findings:
    *   Using harmonized segregation indices for strategic selection of urban areas for in-depth qualitative or longitudinal studies.
    *   Leveraging the comprehensive analysis of correlates as a starting point for causal research on segregation dynamics and its co-evolution with other segregation dimensions.
    *   Investigating the consequences of residential segregation by examining whether differences in segregation levels translate into diverging lived experiences and integration outcomes for immigrants.
*   **Methodology - Data:**
    *   **Functional Urban Areas (FUAs):** The study uses the Eurostat/OECD classification of FUAs, defined by an urban center and its commuting zone, to identify urban areas across Europe. This approach aims to standardize urban area definitions and avoid country-specific variations.
    *   **Local Native and Immigrant Population Data:** Data from 2021/2022 censuses are used, harmonized to a 1x1 km grid cell level across 30 countries. Special attention is given to harmonizing data for the UK from multiple sources.
    *   **FUA and Country-Level Correlates:** Information is collected from various sources (Eurostat, OECD, UN, etc.) to examine correlates of segregation at both FUA and country levels. Missing values are handled through imputation.
*   **Methodology - Measures:**
    *   **Spatial Dissimilarity Index (eD):** The primary measure of segregation is the spatial dissimilarity index, which captures the unevenness of immigrant and native distribution across urban areas, accounting for geographic locality. The index is scale-invariant and comparable across different population sizes. A 1km radius is used for defining local neighborhoods.
    *   **Spatial Isolation Index (meP\*):** In addition to unevenness, the study also analyzes isolation, which measures the extent to which immigrants are exposed to other immigrants in their local environments.
*   **Methodology - Statistical Methods:**
    *   **Specification Curve Analysis:** This method is employed to identify robust associations between FUA and country characteristics and residential segregation.
    *   **Regression Models:** For urban area-level analysis, regression models with country fixed effects are used, including basic population controls and sets of additional FUA-level variables.
    *   **Multilevel Models:** For country-level analysis, random-effects multilevel models are used, incorporating FUA-level controls, additional FUA characteristics, and country-level characteristics.
    *   **Statistical Significance Tests:** Three tests are described to assess the statistical significance of variables, including a test for robust association direction, a comparison of median estimates to bootstrapped counterfactuals, and a test of whether observed estimates fall outside the 95% quantile range of counterfactual estimates.

nodes.title: Table S1: Summary of variables used in the Specification Curve Analysis
nodes.summary:
This partial document, titled "E Variable definitions" and featuring "Table S1: Summary of variables used in the Specification Curve Analysis," outlines a comprehensive set of variables categorized into several key groups: Population Characteristics, Economic Conditions, Housing Market, Migrants' Characteristics, and Country Characteristics.

Within **Population Characteristics**, variables cover aspects like population dispersion (normalized Shannon entropy), population density, population size, and demographic makeup including the proportion of immigrants and educational attainment levels (% High education, % Medium education). It also includes a variable for % Far-right vote.

**Economic Conditions** are detailed through performance indicators such as GDP per capita and unemployment rate. It also includes measures of poverty risk and income inequality (Income ratio 1st/5th quintile). The composition of employment is examined with % Employment industry and % Employment service. A significant focus is placed on native-immigrant inequality, with variables measuring ratios of mean ISEI, high ISCO codes, medium ISCO codes, and unemployment rates between immigrant and native populations.

The **Housing Market** section addresses affordability (Mean apartment price), housing cost burden (% overbudend housing cost), turnover (% homeowners, % same residence last year), tightness (dwellings occupied, dwellings per 1000 residents), and recency of construction (% dwellings built after 2001).

**Migrants' Characteristics** delve into migration flow (% from abroad since last year, % migrants since 2010, % migrants since 2000) and immigrant composition based on origin (EU, Western, MENA, Sub-saharan African, Asian, Latin-American) and income level (% Lower-income migrants, % Lower-medium income migrants).

Finally, **Country Characteristics** include welfare state indicators (% social expenditure), housing policy measures (% social housing expenditure, % with housing allowance), migration stock (specifically % immigrants before 2000), and an incorporation index (MIPEX) that measures immigrant rights across various domains.

Each variable is described with its name, a clear description, the geographical level of analysis (FUA, NUTS3, NUTS2, country), and the year of data collection.
